sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to give tzedaka to every Jew who needs it, as it is said (Devarim 15:7-8): "If there be among you a needy man, one of your brothers, within any of your gates in your land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your needy brother. But you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need in that which he lacks." And when we read the verses precisely, we find that one who can give tzedaka and does not give, in addition to neglecting a positive commandment, also transgresses a prohibition, as it is said (Devarim 15:7): "You shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your needy brother."

The mitzva of tzedaka is one of the great mitzvot of the Torah, and the Sages said of it: "Tzedaka is equal to all the mitzvot" (Bava Batra 9a). And one who gives tzedaka cleaves to the trait of the Holy One, blessed be He, who gives life to and sustains His creatures. And since tzedaka adds life to the world, it therefore saves from death, as it is said: "And tzedaka saves from death" (Mishlei 10:2).

The mitzva of tzedaka is not optional but an obligation that the Torah places on every individual and on society as a whole. Its purpose is to help and support the sick and the elderly, orphans and widows, who cannot sustain themselves. And one who evades fulfilling the obligation of tzedaka is considered as though he worships idols (Bava Batra 10a), for he resigns himself to the deficiencies that exist in the world, in the manner of idol worshippers, who do not believe in the possibility of repairing the world. And the Sages said: "Whoever sustains one soul of Israel, Scripture considers it as though he sustained an entire world" (Mishna Sanhedrin 4:5). And by grappling with the difficulties that exist in the world, and helping those who suffer and the wretched, we repair the world and bring the redemption nearer, as the Sages said: "Great is tzedaka, for it brings the redemption near, as it is said (Yeshayahu 56): Thus says the Lord: Keep justice and do righteousness (tzedaka), for My salvation is near to come and My righteousness to be revealed" (Bava Batra 10a).

The aim of tzedaka is to help our brothers survive in a dignified way. Therefore the highest level of tzedaka is to help the poor person stand on his feet by his own strength, so that he will no longer need to ask for tzedaka, as it is said (Vayikra 25:35): "And if your brother becomes poor and his hand falters with you, you shall uphold him." For example, one who helps a poor person find a steady job, or who makes sure that he learns a profession from which he can afterwards earn a living with dignity, fulfils the mitzva of tzedaka in the most excellent way, because this is the most dignified and effective way to bring the poor person out of the cycle of poverty.

And when there is no possibility of helping the poor person stand on his feet by his own strength – either because we do not have the ability to find him work or to teach him a profession, or because the poor person is sick and unable to work – then the mitzva is to take care of his sustenance. And the more dignified the way in which the help is given to him, the more excellent the tzedaka; and the more the tzedaka is given to him in a way that shames him, the lower its level (see SA YD 249:6-13).

In order to fulfil the mitzva of tzedaka, the members of the communities would appoint tzedaka gabba'im, and the gabba'im had a tzedaka fund, and they would collect tzedaka from all the members of the community who were able to give. And from the fund they would support the poor of the town and give them their basic needs (SA YD siman 256).

Question: Who is a poor person to whom tzedaka must be given? Does it depend on the poor person's own feeling, or are there fixed rules?

Answer: As a rule, a poor person is one who is unable to buy the things considered basic by the great majority of the population in the country where he lives. But in special cases there is also personal poverty – of a person who was accustomed to a life of comfort and lost his wealth, and finds it very hard to get used to his new situation; and the mitzva is to help him for a certain time to maintain his former routine of life until he gets used to his new financial situation.

And this is what is said (Devarim 15:7-8): "If there be among you a needy man… you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your needy brother. But you shall surely open your hand to him… sufficient for his need in that which he lacks."

The Sages said: if there was a wealthy man who was accustomed to go out riding on a horse with a servant running before him, and he lost his wealth, they give him a horse and a servant. "They said of Hillel the Elder that he took for a certain poor man of good family a horse to ride on and a servant to run before him. Once he did not find a servant to run before him, and he ran before him for three mil" (Ketubot 67b). And likewise, if he was accustomed to dress in expensive clothes and eat expensive food – they give it to him, as it is said "that which he lacks" – "he": according to his situation and habit. For if he was wealthy and became accustomed to a life of splendour and comfort, and lost his wealth, he will suffer so much from their absence that perhaps he will die of heartache.

But this must be limited by two principles. a) If there are poorer people who have not yet received their basic needs, they should be given precedence, for this is the rule: the poorer comes first. Therefore, only after the basic needs of all the poor have been supplied – in food, clothing, housing and the education of children – and there is still the possibility of giving more tzedaka from the public fund or from private people, is there an obligation to give the wealthy man his need, "that which he lacks". b) One must educate the wealthy man who lost his wealth to live simply, so that he does not become a heavy burden on the public, which would have to supply him all his life with a horse to ride and a servant to run before him. For all that we were commanded is to ease his descent until he gets used to a simple life. And perhaps, if we help the wealthy man who lost his wealth to keep his status for a certain period, he will be able to rebuild his business and stand on his feet. But if it becomes clear that his business is lost, he must get used to a simple life.

And as for Hillel the Elder running before that poor man of good family, this was apparently beyond the letter of the law, in keeping with the special way of Hillel the Elder, who was accustomed to forgo his own honour. And perhaps that poor man of good family was in such a difficult state of mind that Hillel the Elder knew that if he did not honour him, he might die of grief. And who knows, perhaps after that run of Hillel the Elder, that poor man reflected in his heart that it was not fitting for him to continue pampering himself so much, and he made peace with his new situation and took upon himself to live simply from then on.

sections.title_en: 3. Tzedaka Through Wise and Upright Gabba'im
sections.body_en:
Question: How is it preferable to distribute tzedaka – through gabba'im, or should each person decide for himself to whom to give tzedaka?

Answer: The proper order is to give tzedaka through wise and upright tzedaka gabba'im (see SA YD 249:7; 257:1-2). For one who does not know how to help the poor may unintentionally deepen their distress: instead of encouraging them to work, he will accustom them to prefer the easy money that comes from tzedaka over the hard money that comes from work. But in truth this will not do him good; on the contrary, he will be lowly in his own eyes and in the eyes of his family. Such an existence will influence him for the worse, and may develop a spoiled character in his children.

And one who does not know the poor person well may be mistaken about a poor person who is not upright, who begs for alms because he is addicted to gambling or drugs or alcohol. And one who gives tzedaka to poor people who are not upright has no reward for a mitzva (Bava Kamma 16b).

But wise and upright tzedaka gabba'im know how to help upright poor people effectively. Sometimes the gabbai must make the giving of tzedaka conditional on the poor person working, and for every shekel he earns they will add him another shekel. Sometimes they need to find him work for which the employer is willing to pay two thousand shekels a month, and add to it, without his knowing, another two thousand shekels from tzedaka funds, so that he and his family will think that it is he who supports the family by his devoted work. In this way they will help both his material survival and his moral standing in his own eyes and his family's.

And even when we are speaking of a person who is entirely unable to work and whose family's needs are many, and who must be helped on an ongoing basis with tzedaka, nevertheless the tzedaka gabba'im must supervise that the tzedaka they give him is used properly – for food and clothing, and the education of the children in Torah and derekh eretz – and not for buying luxuries or for gambling or strong drink. In cases where there is a concern that the money will go to unnecessary or harmful needs, it is forbidden to give him money, only provisions.

And if there is a poor person who needs to be helped, but because of his moral sensitivity he is not interested in receiving help, one must appease him with words and tell him that everything is from Heaven, and the wheel turns in the world; and if he were wealthy, he would certainly help his friends; therefore, now that he is poor, he should accept tzedaka, and look at the beautiful aspects of his life and rejoice in them, and know that everything is for the good.

The general principle: it is right to give tzedaka through wise and upright people who know how to help the poor, and they are the tzedaka gabba'im. And the Sages alluded to this too when they said: "The poor of your own town come first." In addition to the moral obligation towards those close to us coming first, the poor of the town are known, and one can help them in a more correct way.

When possible, it is good that the tzedaka gabba'im work in full cooperation with educators and the staff of the welfare department; in this way, together, with the national and local resources, they will be able to help the poor in the most effective way. But it must be noted that, regrettably, sometimes welfare workers do not properly understand their work, or do not know well those who need their services, or are not diligent enough to cooperate with the forces on the ground. And then there is no choice but to act in the best way possible with the forces in the community, while hoping that the welfare workers will not interfere.

sections.title_en: 4. How Much to Give a Poor Person Who Goes from Door to Door
sections.body_en:
Question: How much tzedaka is it fitting to give a poor person who knocks on the door of the house and asks for tzedaka?

Answer: In the Talmud (Bava Batra 9a) it is explained that it is not fitting to give a large gift to a poor person who goes from door to door, but on the other hand one should not send him away with nothing; rather, one must give him a small gift, that is, an amount with which one can buy something to eat. In our days this can be estimated at half a shekel. And some say that the amount of a peruta, which is about two agorot, is enough, and since there is no such coin, he should give five or ten agorot.

And not more than this, for since he has become accustomed to going from door to door, who knows how much he will collect; and perhaps he no longer needs it so much and nevertheless continues to collect tzedaka, and causes people to stumble in giving tzedaka to a poor person who is not upright. And one who gives tzedaka to poor people who are not upright has no reward for a mitzva (Bava Kamma 16b).

And even if the one who goes from door to door truly needs tzedaka, it is not clear that he should be given precedence, for according to the rules of halakha one should give precedence to the poor who are relatives and neighbours, and who knows whether the one who goes from door to door needs tzedaka more than they do.

And even if he has in his hand a letter of recommendation from important rabbis, this still does not mean that he is more in need than the local tzedaka fund, or the institutions of Torah and kindness close to the donor's place and heart.

Therefore it is fitting for every person to distribute the tithe of money from his profits and salary according to his own judgement, and with this he fulfils his obligation of the mitzva of tzedaka; and to those poor people who go from door to door he should give a small gift.

sections.title_en: 5. The Order of Precedence in Tzedaka
sections.body_en:
Question: The needs of the poor are many; how should a person determine to whom to give tzedaka?

Answer: There are three principles in the order of precedence, and they are the same principles we learned in the mitzva of lending (chapter 5, halakhot 11 and 13).

The three principles are alluded to in the verse (Devarim 15:7): "If there be among you a needy man, one of your brothers, within any of your gates in your land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your needy brother." The first principle is "needy": the more needy, that is, the one more in need of help, should be given precedence. Therefore one should give precedence to one who needs food over one who needs clothing, and to one who needs clothing over one who needs furniture. The second principle: "one of your brothers" – the one who is considered more "your brother" should be given precedence. Therefore parents come before grown children, children before brothers, brothers before uncles, and uncles before cousins. The third principle: "within any of your gates" – the poor of your own town come before the poor of another town. When there is a clash between two principles, the first principle comes before the second, and the second before the third (as explained above, 5:13). We learned another halakha from the verse: that the poor of the Land of Israel come before the poor outside the Land, as it is said: "in your land which the Lord your God gives you" (SA 251:3).

It must further be added that a good friend too is considered like a relative who should be given precedence. And likewise ideological closeness is considered closeness; therefore a person who wants to donate to yeshivot – since many yeshiva students are considered poor during their years of study in the yeshiva – should give precedence to yeshivot close to his worldview over yeshivot far from his worldview.

It is important to note that there are situations in which the guidance of halakha is clear and decisive, and then one must not deviate from it. For example, when both the brother and the cousin need tzedaka, and both are in a similar financial situation, it is clear that one should give precedence to the brother. And likewise, when the brother needs a little help, while the cousin is about to die of hunger, it is clear that the cousin comes first. But when the cousin needs help more than the brother, but the difference between them is not great, here the guidance of halakha is not decisive, and in such a case each person must decide for himself whom to prefer. And in general one must know that many times it is hard to determine who is more needy, because people and their needs are very different from one another. And in all these cases a person must decide according to his judgement and the inclination of his heart, and sometimes, in order to decide correctly, he must consult a wise person.

Just as in all the laws of tzedaka and kindness one should give precedence to the one who is closer, as it is said (Shemot 22:24): "to the poor person with you," and the one who is more "with you" comes first, so too a person who is undecided to which yeshivot to donate should give precedence and donate to the yeshivot that are closer to him.

And there are several kinds of closeness: personal closeness, ideological closeness and closeness of place.

A person who studied in a certain yeshiva – his closeness to that yeshiva is personal closeness; he himself studied there, and certainly he should give it precedence over the other yeshivot, and set aside the first part of his donation for its benefit. And especially today, when most of those who study in yeshivot do not pay a sum that covers the expenses the yeshiva spends on them; and of course, first of all the students bear a moral obligation to return to the yeshiva what it spent on them. And it is fitting that every student make an account for himself of roughly how much money was spent on him during his years in the yeshiva, and make an effort to return the whole sum to the yeshiva.

And there is also ideological closeness. The Torah is broader than the sea, and every yeshiva has some special emphasis. Some emphasise joy more, and some musar. Some emphasise love of the Land, and some love of the People. There are yeshivot that emphasise their connection to the settlement of the Land, to the army, to the ingathering of the exiles, and there are yeshivot that emphasise these aspects less. There are yeshivot that emphasise the difference between religious and secular, and there are yeshivot that emphasise what all Israel has in common. And each person should donate to the yeshiva or yeshivot that are closer to his spirit and his worldview. And there is no division in this; on the contrary, through the multiplicity of opinions and ideas the Torah appears in greater completeness. And each one should be faithful to his worldview, and for the sake of Heaven, out of love of Israel, help the yeshiva that suits his outlook.

And the third and last closeness in order of importance is closeness of place. One who is undecided between two yeshivot, both of which are close to his spirit, but one is in another town and the second in his own town, should certainly give precedence to the yeshiva in his own town.

And thank God, in our times the poor have greatly decreased, and in the State of Israel too a number of laws have been enacted that greatly help families in distress. Therefore the great sages of our generation have written and said that generally the most excellent tzedaka today is a donation to a yeshiva, for thereby one strengthens the inner, spiritual side of Israel. And further, the young men who study in a yeshiva are considered poor, since on the one hand they have not yet managed to establish their financial position, and on the other hand, since they are adults, their parents are not obligated to support and maintain them.

Question: Is a person obligated to set aside a tithe from the money he earns?

Answer: The halakha is that the choicest way of the mitzva is to give a fifth of one's profits to tzedaka, the average measure is to give a tenth of one's profits, and one who gives less fulfils the mitzva of tzedaka in the manner of a begrudging eye (SA YD 249:1).

The poskim disagreed about the question of the source of the mitzva to give a tithe of money (ma'aser kesafim). In the view of a minority of poskim the obligation is from the Torah (so it is implied by Tosafot, Ta'anit 9a). Some hold that the obligation is rabbinic (Taz YD 331:32). And some hold that the obligation is by force of custom (Baḥ there).

But it must be emphasised that although some say that the source of ma'aser kesafim is custom, this does not mean that one who gives a tithe fulfils a light mitzva whose foundation is in custom. For it is clear that the mitzva of tzedaka itself is from the Torah, as it is said (Devarim 15:7-8): "You shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your needy brother. But you shall surely open your hand to him… sufficient for his need in that which he lacks." That is, when possible, one must supply the needs of each and every poor person, "sufficient for his need in that which he lacks". But generally the needs of the poor are many, and there is no possibility of supplying everyone's needs; therefore halakha established that the average measure is to give a tenth. It turns out, then, that the mitzva to give a tithe of money is the definition of how to fulfil the Torah's mitzva at the average measure.

That is, although some say that the source of giving a tithe is custom, the custom comes to interpret the Torah's mitzva, and one who gives less than a tenth does not fulfil the Torah's mitzva even at the average measure, but in the manner of one with a begrudging eye.

Nevertheless, there is a halakhic significance to the question of the source of the obligation to give ma'aser kesafim, and it concerns a person whose financial situation is tight. For if we rule that giving ma'aser kesafim is from the Torah – even when his situation is tight, as long as he is not compelled by circumstances, he is obligated to give a tithe to someone poorer than he or to support Torah study. But if we rule in accordance with the view of most poskim that giving ma'aser kesafim was defined by the Sages – then one whose situation is tight is exempt from giving a tithe and may make do with giving a small gift to someone poorer than he, but one whose situation is somewhat tight will be obligated in ma'aser kesafim. And if we rule that giving ma'aser kesafim is a custom, then even one whose situation is slightly tight will be exempt from ma'aser kesafim, and the custom applies only to an ordinary person earning an average living.

sections.title_en: 8. Tithe So That You Become Rich
sections.body_en:
Question: Is it true that one who sets aside ma'aser kesafim is promised that he will become rich through it?

Answer: The Sages expounded the verse (Devarim 14:22): "'Aser te'aser' (you shall surely tithe) – tithe so that you become rich (titasher)." And so Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei explained that the rich of the Land of Israel became rich because they set aside tithes (Shabbat 119a). And it is explained in the Talmud (Ta'anit 9a) that although in general it is forbidden to test the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Devarim 6:16): "You shall not test the Lord your God as you tested Him at Massah," nevertheless in this matter – that a person set aside a tithe and thereby become rich – one may test the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Malakhi 3:10): "Bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house, and test Me now with this, says the Lord of hosts, if I will not open for you the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing until there is no room to receive it."

And so the Rema wrote (YD 247:4) in practice, that one who gives ma'aser kesafim becomes rich, and it is permitted to test Hashem in this. But the Shelah (tractate Megilla, Ner Mitzva 22) wrote that the author of the Shulḥan Arukh did not mention this, because in his view it is forbidden to test Hashem with ma'aser kesafim; and what they expounded on the verse "aser te'aser" means that one who gives the tithe of grain, wine and oil, whose mitzva is from the Torah, becomes rich. And about this it is said in Malakhi that one may test Hashem; but not in giving tzedaka. Therefore the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 247:2-4) wrote several virtues of tzedaka: "A person never becomes poor from tzedaka, and no evil thing and no harm comes about through it. Whoever has mercy on the poor, the Holy One, blessed be He, has mercy on him. Tzedaka repels harsh decrees, and in famine it saves from death," but he did not write that the one who tithes becomes rich and that one may test Hashem in this. And so wrote Responsa She'ilat Ya'avetz (1:3).

But most poskim wrote that one may test Hashem with ma'aser kesafim. And so wrote the book Ahavat Ḥesed (part 2, 18), and he proved that the verse in Malakhi speaks of rabbinic tithes: for at the beginning of the days of the Second Temple, when the prophet Malakhi prophesied, most Jews did not live in the Land, and consequently setting aside terumot and ma'aserot was rabbinic; and nevertheless he prophesied that one may test Hashem in this. Thus even with ma'aser kesafim, which is not from the Torah, one may test Hashem.

However, it seems that the meaning is a hidden miracle, that is, that Hashem will send blessing into the work of his hands; but the meaning is not that one who behaves negligently and without understanding will become rich despite all his desires and mistakes.

And one may ask: is it fitting for a person to do a mitzva in order to become rich, and why does the Torah guide us, "tithe so that you become rich"? But indeed it is so: it is good that those who give a tithe become rich, and then they will give more tithes and be partners in repairing the world. In addition, there is a sanctification of Hashem's Name in the givers of tzedaka being rich.

sections.title_en: 9. Which Money Is Subject to Ma'aser Kesafim?
sections.body_en:
Question: Must one set aside a tithe only from money one earns, or must one set aside a tithe also from money one receives as a gift?
Answer: The mitzva to give ma'aser kesafim applies to all money that reaches a person – whether money he received as an inheritance, or money he earned as salary or in trade, or money he received as a gift from relatives or friends, or grants that various bodies award, or severance pay at the end of his employment; from all these monies one must set aside ma'aser kesafim.

Question: Must one set aside a tithe from gifts received for a wedding?
Answer: Some hold that even one who received a gift worth money, such as a refrigerator, must give a tithe of its value to tzedaka (Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach). But the accepted ruling is that one need set aside a tithe only from money. Therefore, a bride and groom who received various gifts and money must set aside a tithe from the money only.

Question: Parents who gave their married daughter money so that she would buy herself a dress – must she set aside a tithe from the money?
Answer: She need not set aside a tithe from the money, because the gift is not money but a dress. And if change remains, and her parents' intention is that she may use the change as she sees fit, she should set aside a tithe from the change. And likewise parents who help their children buy an apartment – the children need not set aside a tithe from the money they received, because their gift is part of an apartment and not money.

Question: Children who receive pocket money from their parents – must they set aside a tithe from it?
Answer: If a child is given pocket money, this implies that he already has the responsibility to use the money as he wishes and that he has reached the age of education; therefore he should be educated in the mitzva and set aside a tithe. And although the parents already set aside a tithe from the money when they received it, since it passed into the child's hands, he must set it aside. However, all this is on condition that the money was given to the child for free use; but if the parents gave him money for travel or for buying a garment or a certain device, he need not set aside a tithe from it. Only if change remains and the parents agree that their son use it as he wishes should he set aside a tithe from the change.

Question: Must a soldier set aside a tithe from the money he receives from the army?
Answer: Yes – unless he is poor and lacks basic needs, in which case he is exempt from setting aside a tithe.

Question: Must one set aside a tithe from a birth grant or child allowance, or are they intended for the children?
Answer: Since they are intended for free use as the parents wish, one must set aside a tithe from them.

Question: A person who receives a salary – should he set aside the tithe from the gross or from the net?
Answer: One must set it aside from the net, for that is the money he receives.

Question: Does one set aside a tithe from the whole net, or may one deduct the mortgage payment and the municipal tax from the salary and set aside a tithe from the remainder?
Answer: One must set aside a tithe from the whole net; what a person pays for the mortgage and municipal tax is already considered part of his ongoing expenses, which are not deducted from the salary.

Question: A person who spends money on travel to work, and on food he buys at work – may he deduct these expenses from the net he received?
Answer: One may deduct the cost of travel to work from the salary and set aside a tithe from the rest, because were it not for the need to get to work he would not travel there. But buying food during work hours is not considered a work expense, since in any case he would have needed to eat.

Question: How should a person who saves money in a savings plan or a provident fund set aside a tithe?
Answer: First he must set aside a tithe from the money before he deposits it in the savings plan. Afterwards, when the time of redemption comes, he should calculate how much real profit he had on the savings, and set aside a tithe from that. And likewise one who invests his money in a provident fund must set aside a tithe from the money before depositing it, and when he redeems his money in the provident fund, he should calculate the real profit he had over the years and set aside a tithe from that.

However, many times employers, as part of the benefits they give employees, deposit money into provident funds, and then the money does not pass through the employee's current account, and it is hard to calculate the amount of the tithe. Therefore, when he withdraws the money from the provident fund, he should set aside a tithe from all of it.

Question: How should one who invested his money in shares, some of which made a profit and some a loss, set aside a tithe?
Answer: He should make an overall calculation: if on the whole he profited, he should set aside a tithe from the profit; and if on the whole he lost, he is exempt from setting aside a tithe. And only after he covers his losses and begins to profit will he again be obligated to set aside ma'aser kesafim.

Question: If a person has occasion to donate a large sum to tzedaka, much more than he needs to set aside for ma'aser kesafim, may he consider the donation as a loan to the tithe?
Answer: Yes. For example, one who needs to set aside a thousand shekels every month and gave ten thousand to tzedaka at once may consider the ten thousand shekels as a debt of the "ma'aser kesafim", and for the ten months he will not set aside a tithe from his salary.

Question: Is it fitting to be precise in calculating ma'aser kesafim from every income, or may one calculate it approximately?
Answer: It is preferable to calculate ma'aser kesafim precisely, and in order to calculate precisely one should dedicate a notebook or ledger to this. Indeed, one who is sure that he gives at least a tenth can fulfil the mitzva even without a precise calculation. But some say that the segula that brings wealth applies specifically when one calculates precisely; therefore it is preferable to keep a precise record, and if he wishes to add afterwards, let him add. And we have already learned that the measure of a generous eye is to set aside a fifth.

sections.title_en: 11. For Which Purposes May Ma'aser Kesafim Be Given?
sections.body_en:
Question: May one donate ma'aser kesafim money to building a synagogue?
Answer: Some say that ma'aser kesafim money must be directed to tzedaka for the poor, and best of all to poor Torah learners, but it is forbidden to direct it to other mitzva needs, such as building a synagogue (Maharil, as cited in the Rema YD 249:1). And some say that it is permitted to use the tithe money also for other mitzva needs, such as building a synagogue or buying books for the synagogue (Maharam, as cited in the Maharshal and the Shakh 249:3). And if the person who began setting aside a tithe took it upon himself to give it to the poor, according to all views he is forbidden to give it to other mitzva needs.

And the custom in practice is that one may give the tithe also to other mitzva needs, such as building a synagogue or settling the Land, but ideally one should prefer to give it to the poor or to Torah learners.

Question: Is it permitted to buy holy books with tithe money, and to write on them that they are from tithe money and anyone who wishes may study in them?
Answer: Indeed in the past, several poskim wrote that in a time of need one may buy holy books with ma'aser kesafim money, and write on them that they were bought with tithe money, so that everyone will know that they are permitted to study in them (Shakh 249:3, Taz 1). But they spoke at a time when books were worth a monthly salary, and one who bought a book and was ready to lend it to others did great kindness by this, and many were helped by it for real study. And although some are lenient in this even today, it seems that in practice, today, when books are cheap, there is no public need in this, and therefore one should not buy holy books with tithe money for one's own study. However, one who wants to study a certain book, and if he sets aside a tithe for tzedaka he will not be able to buy this book, and he truly wants to study it – he is defined as poor and is exempt from setting aside a tithe; and if he wants to be meticulous, he can write that it is from ma'aser kesafim money, so that he will try to lend it to others, or after a time donate it to a beit midrash.

Question: May a person buy tefillin and mezuzot for himself with ma'aser kesafim money?
Answer: It is forbidden to pay with ma'aser kesafim money for mitzvot that a person must fulfil. Therefore a person is forbidden to buy tefillin and mezuzot for himself with ma'aser kesafim money; but it is permitted to buy them for a poor person.

Question: Is it permitted to give the money for the two gifts to the poor on Purim from tithe money?
Answer: Since it is an obligation, it is forbidden to give it from ma'aser kesafim. But one must know that the obligation is to give on Purim about a peruta to each poor person, and some say an amount with which one can buy bread; in any case we are speaking of a few shekels. And if a person wants to add and give a higher sum on Purim for gifts to the poor, he may give it from ma'aser kesafim.

Question: May one give the money for the half-shekel that is customarily given before Purim, or the kapparot money before Yom Kippur, from ma'aser kesafim money?
Answer: Since by custom one must give these gifts to the poor, one should not pay them from the tithe money. But one who is hard-pressed may give them from the tithe money, since there is no absolute obligation to give them.

sections.title_en: 12. Questions from People Who Find It Hard to Set Aside a Tithe
sections.body_en:
Question: When a person is in a tight situation for a certain time, must he take a loan in order to give ma'aser kesafim? Answer: He should postpone giving ma'aser kesafim until his situation improves, and record in his ledger every month how much he owes to the tithe, and in the end pay off his whole debt. For example, one who owes money to his friend, and cannot both repay his debt and set aside ma'aser kesafim, would do better to pay his debt to his friend first, and postpone the payment of his tithes to tzedaka by a few months.

Question: Must one donate the tithe when one is in the minus at the bank?
Answer: As a rule one should not be in the minus at the bank. Some say there is a prohibition of interest in this (above 5:5), and certainly there is no wisdom in it. Therefore one should first cover the minus and afterwards give the tithe. However, one who is unable to restrain himself from spending his money, and is always in the minus, should give ma'aser kesafim even when he is in the minus, so that the ma'aser kesafim will not be less important than all the luxuries because of which he goes into the minus.

Question: A poor person who does not manage to supply his family's basic needs – must he record in his ledger everything he earned, and enter the tithe as a debt, so that if he becomes rich he will donate it to tzedaka? Or is he completely exempt, and even if he becomes rich he will not need to pay a tithe for the period when he was poor?
Answer: A poor person is completely exempt from ma'aser kesafim, and only when Hashem enlarges his borders will he begin to set aside a tithe from his profits.

Question: Instead of giving a tithe, may I carry out electrical work for a yeshiva to which I want to donate? And how should I value the cost of my work – at the standard rate or at a discounted rate?
Answer: If it is work for which that institution would have had to pay money, then your work is worth money, and you may count your work as payment in place of the tithe. And the cost of the work should be calculated at the discounted rate, for so it is accepted between people who have a good relationship, that they do work for one another at a discounted rate. And further, there is concern that the evil inclination will tilt the calculation upwards, in order to be exempt from paying a tithe; and in order to be sure that the calculation is fair, one should go to the other side, according to a discounted rate. It must also be noted that since this is work for which he could have received money, he should count as the tithe only ninety percent of the value of the work, since he would in any case have had to pay a tithe on that work.

sections.title_en: 13. May One Pay the Children's Expenses from Tithe Money?
sections.body_en:
Question: May parents count what they spend on their young children as their ma'aser kesafim?
Answer: Until the age of six, parents are obligated by Torah law to support their children, and the Sages added and obligated the parents to support the children until they reach about the age of thirteen (Ketubot 49b). And since this is an obligation, what is spent on them should not be counted as tzedaka. And one whose situation is very tight, and who cannot support them without the help of the tithe money, is considered poor and is exempt from setting aside ma'aser kesafim.

Question: May parents pay the expenses of their children who have passed the age of mitzvot from tithe money?
Answer: Indeed, by what the Sages enacted there is no obligation to support children who have passed the age of thirteen; but by the aim of the enactment, which was intended to take care of the children's support until they reach the stage at which they can, with difficulty, manage by their own strength, there is room to continue to support them afterwards too (see Igrot Moshe YD 1:143; 2:113). And so too is the law of the State, that parents are obligated to support the children until the age of eighteen. Therefore the children's support after the age of thirteen should not be financed from tithe money. However, one who is hard-pressed may count what he spends on his children who have passed the age of mitzvot as ma'aser kesafim.

Question: May one pay for the sons' Talmud Torah from the tithe money?
Answer: Since it is a mitzva from the Torah that the father is obligated to teach his son Torah or to hire a teacher for him who will teach him Torah, and to keep his children from going astray (see Igrot Moshe YD 2:113), one should not fulfil this obligation with ma'aser kesafim money. However, if the sons are older, and the parents pay for their teachers and also for their food and clothing, and their situation is tight, they may count what they pay for their food and clothing from ma'aser kesafim. And likewise, when they live in a dormitory, it is permitted to pay for the dormitory from ma'aser kesafim (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Laws of Torah Study 1:7).

sections.title_en: 14. May One Help Grown and Married Children from the Tithe?
sections.body_en:
Question: May parents help their children who have passed the age of eighteen, single or married, from their tithe money?
Answer: If the children are considered poor at that time, that is, without this they do not have enough for their basic needs, what is given to them may be counted as ma'aser kesafim. But if the parents are well established and give their children their needs in abundance, their children are not considered poor, and one should not give them from ma'aser kesafim money.

For example, if they buy cheap clothes and economise on all their expenses, the children may be considered poor, and consequently what is given to help them may be counted as tithe money. But if they live in relative comfort – for example, they buy expensive clothes, or they spend money on outings to restaurants – they are not considered poor, and what is spent on them should not be counted as ma'aser kesafim.

And likewise regarding children who have married: if they keep a car, it is clear that they are not considered poor, and what is given to them should not be counted as ma'aser kesafim. And likewise if they bought expensive furniture, they are not considered poor, for if they were poor they would buy second-hand or simple furniture. And likewise if the parents bought them an apartment, or they rent a relatively expensive apartment, for example in a city rather than in a settlement, they cannot be considered poor.

The general principle: parents may count help to children who have passed the age of eighteen only on condition that they live frugally. And then the payment for their food, clothes and travel can be counted as ma'aser kesafim. And likewise the payment for their professional studies at university can be counted as ma'aser kesafim, for thereby they will afterwards be able to support themselves with dignity; and we have already learned (in halakha 1) that the greatest tzedaka is to help the poor person stand on his feet by his own strength. And likewise what is paid to a yeshiva gevoha, where the main payment is for the dormitory, can be counted as ma'aser kesafim. But if the children do not live frugally but as is customary in society, their standing is more or less like that of ordinary people, and consequently they are not considered poor, and what is given to them should not be counted as ma'aser kesafim.

Question: When a person is in a situation where both his parents need help and his grown children need help, and he is not able to help them all, whom should he help? Answer: Parents come before children (Rema YD 251:3).

Question: May one give the tithe money to needy parents? Answer: If the son has the possibility of supporting his needy parents, he is obligated to support them. And the Sages said that if he gives his tzedaka money to his parents, a curse (me'era) will come upon him, for it is not fitting to give them tzedaka; rather, it is fitting to share his personal money with them. But if his situation is such that without the ma'aser kesafim money he will not be able to help his parents, then parents come before children and before all other poor people, and therefore he should give them the tithe money (SA and Rema YD 240:5).
